questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Which transponder code tells air traffic services you have an emergency?
questions.explain: 7700 is the emergency code. 7600 is radio failure and 7500 is unlawful interference.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Two aircraft are converging at about the same level. Which one gives way?
options: The one that has the other on its right
The one that has the other on its left
questions.explain: The aircraft that has the other on its right gives way, normally by turning right.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Two aircraft are approaching head-on. What should each pilot do?
questions.explain: Both alter heading to the right so they pass left side to left side.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: You are overtaking another aircraft in flight. How should you pass?
options: Pass on its right, keeping clear
It must move aside for you
questions.explain: The overtaking aircraft keeps out of the way and passes by altering heading to the right.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: In flight you see a steady red light from the tower aimed at you. What does it mean?
options: Give way to other aircraft and continue circling
Return to the aerodrome and land
questions.explain: Steady red in flight means give way and keep circling. Flashing red means the aerodrome is unsafe, do not land.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: On the ground you see a flashing green light from the tower. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Flashing green on the ground means cleared to taxi. Steady green means cleared for take-off.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: A powered aeroplane and a glider are converging. Which normally gives way?
questions.explain: Powered aircraft give way to gliders, balloons and airships, which are less able to manoeuvre.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: On the ground you see a flashing white light from the tower. What should you do?
options: Taxi clear of the landing area
Return to the starting point on the aerodrome
questions.explain: Flashing white to an aircraft on the ground means return to the starting point on the aerodrome.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Why is hypoxia particularly dangerous?
options: Its early effects can go unnoticed while judgement is impaired
questions.explain: Hypoxia is insidious. Euphoria and impaired judgement can set in before you recognise anything is wrong.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: You smell exhaust fumes and feel a headache while the cabin heater is on. What is the most likely cause and first action?
options: Carbon monoxide; turn the heater off and open fresh-air vents
questions.explain: Cabin heaters often use heat from around the exhaust, so a leak can bring in carbon monoxide. Turn the heat off and get fresh air.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: After a long, gentle turn you roll wings level and feel you are now turning the other way. What is this?
questions.explain: The inner ear adapts to a steady turn, so rolling level can feel like a turn the other way. Trust the instruments and the horizon.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Another aircraft on a collision course with you will usually appear to…
options: Stay in the same place on the windscreen while growing larger
questions.explain: An object with no relative movement that grows in size is on a collision course. Act early.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What is an effective way to scan for traffic?
options: Short, regularly spaced eye movements, pausing on each section
questions.explain: Eyes detect objects best when stationary, so scan in short steps and pause briefly on each part of the sky.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: In cloud you feel strongly that you are climbing, but the instruments show level flight. What should you do?
questions.explain: Your body’s motion senses are unreliable without visual references. Trust the instruments.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Tingling fingers, dizziness and rapid breathing during a stressful moment most likely suggest…
questions.explain: Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide in the blood. Slow your breathing deliberately, for example by talking.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Why should pilots not fly soon after scuba diving?
options: Reduced cabin pressure raises the risk of decompression sickness
questions.explain: Nitrogen absorbed while diving can form bubbles at the lower pressure of altitude. Follow the recommended waiting time.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which conditions most favour radiation fog?
options: Clear night, light wind and moist air
Warm air over a cold sea
questions.explain: Clear skies let the ground cool overnight; a light wind and moist air let fog form over land.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Advection fog forms when…
options: Air cools on a clear night with no wind
Warm, moist air moves over a colder surface
Air rises up a mountain slope
questions.explain: Advection fog comes from moist air being cooled from below as it moves over a cold surface, and it can persist in wind.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Carburettor icing is most likely when…
options: It is very cold and dry
Humidity is high and the engine is at low power
questions.explain: Carb icing can occur in warm, humid air well above freezing, and it is most likely at low power, such as in a descent.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What are ISA conditions at mean sea level?
questions.explain: The International Standard Atmosphere uses 15 °C and 1013.25 hPa at sea level, cooling about 2 °C per 1,000 ft.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In a METAR, “BKN” cloud cover means…
questions.explain: FEW is 1–2 oktas, SCT 3–4, BKN 5–7 and OVC 8.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which of these is part of “CAVOK”?
options: Visibility 10 km or more and no cloud below 5,000 ft or minimum sector altitude, if higher
questions.explain: CAVOK means visibility 10 km or more, no cloud below 5,000 ft (or MSA if higher), no cumulonimbus or towering cumulus, and no significant weather.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In the northern hemisphere, standing with your back to the wind, low pressure is…
questions.explain: Buys Ballot’s law: in the northern hemisphere, with your back to the wind, low pressure is on your left.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: The temperature and dew point in reports are getting closer together. What should you expect?
options: A higher risk of fog or low cloud
questions.explain: As air cools towards its dew point it nears saturation, so mist, fog or low cloud become more likely.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: As a cold front passes in the northern hemisphere, the wind typically…
questions.explain: Wind usually veers (shifts clockwise) as a cold front passes in the northern hemisphere, often with showers and falling temperature.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “WILCO” mean?
options: I understand your message and will comply
questions.explain: WILCO means “will comply”. ROGER only means you received the message.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “ROGER” mean?
options: I have received all of your last transmission
questions.explain: ROGER acknowledges receipt only. It is not a readback or an agreement to comply.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which call signals grave and imminent danger requiring immediate assistance?
questions.explain: MAYDAY is the distress call. PAN PAN is the urgency call for a serious situation that does not need immediate assistance.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which of these must you read back to ATC?
options: A frequency you will not use
questions.explain: Altimeter settings, runway instructions, headings, levels, SSR codes and frequency changes must be read back.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which international distress frequency is monitored for aircraft emergencies?
questions.explain: 121.5 MHz is the international aeronautical emergency frequency.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which word means “yes” in standard radio phraseology?
questions.explain: ICAO phraseology uses AFFIRM for yes and NEGATIVE for no.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Your radio fails. Which transponder code should you select?
questions.explain: 7600 tells ATC you have lost radio communication.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: A wing stalls when…
options: Airspeed falls below a fixed value
It exceeds its critical angle of attack
The nose is above the horizon
questions.explain: A stall happens at the critical angle of attack, which can be reached at any airspeed or attitude.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In a level 60° banked turn, what is the load factor?
questions.explain: Load factor in a level turn is 1 ÷ cos(bank). At 60° that is 2 g, and stall speed rises by about 41%.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Lowering flap generally…
options: Increases lift and drag and lowers the stall speed
Has no effect on stall speed
questions.explain: Flap increases the wing’s lift and drag, letting you fly slower with a steeper approach.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: What is the main purpose of a trim tab?
options: To relieve control pressure so the aircraft holds an attitude
questions.explain: Trim removes the need to hold a constant force on the controls.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: How does a centre of gravity near the aft limit affect handling?
options: Less stable, lighter elevator forces and harder stall recovery
questions.explain: An aft CG reduces longitudinal stability and can make stall and spin recovery more difficult. Never fly outside the limits.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Close to the ground the aircraft “floats” on landing. Why?
options: Air is denser at ground level only
questions.explain: Within about one wingspan of the ground, ground effect reduces induced drag, so excess speed makes the aircraft float.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Rolling into a turn, the nose briefly yaws away from the turn. What causes this?
options: Adverse yaw from extra drag on the rising wing’s aileron
questions.explain: The down-going aileron on the rising wing creates more drag, yawing the nose away. Use coordinated rudder.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Wake turbulence is strongest behind an aircraft that is…
options: Light, fast and with flaps down
questions.explain: Heavy, slow, clean aircraft produce the strongest wingtip vortices.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Landing behind a large aircraft that has just landed, how can you avoid its wake?
options: Stay below its approach path and land short of its touchdown point
Stay above its approach path and land beyond its touchdown point
Land exactly on its touchdown point
questions.explain: Vortices sink behind the aircraft and stop when it touches down, so stay above its path and land beyond where it touched down.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: A light crosswind on the runway can make wake turbulence more hazardous because…
options: It can hold one vortex over the runway
questions.explain: A light crosswind can keep the upwind vortex stationary over the runway for longer.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: On final approach your airspeed suddenly rises then drops sharply. This most likely indicates…
questions.explain: Sudden airspeed changes on approach suggest wind shear. Be ready to go around.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Taking off after a large aircraft has departed, how should you avoid its wake?
options: Lift off before its rotation point and climb above its path
Lift off after its rotation point and stay below its path
questions.explain: Its vortices start where it rotated, so lift off earlier and climb above its flight path, or wait.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: On a hot day at a high-elevation airfield, what should you expect?
options: Longer take-off run and poorer climb
questions.explain: High density altitude reduces engine, propeller and wing performance.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Which combination gives the highest density altitude?
questions.explain: Heat, low pressure and high elevation all reduce air density. Humidity reduces it a little further.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Which surface increases take-off distance compared with a dry, level, paved runway?
questions.explain: Wet or long grass, uphill slopes, tailwinds and higher mass all increase take-off distance.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How is the centre of gravity position found?
questions.explain: CG arm = total moment ÷ total mass.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: The wind is 20 kt at 30° to the runway. What is the approximate headwind component?
questions.explain: Headwind ≈ 20 × cos 30° ≈ 17 kt. The crosswind component is 20 × sin 30° = 10 kt.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: A pilot of 80 kg sits at an arm of 2.0 m from the datum. What is the moment?
questions.explain: Moment = mass × arm = 80 × 2.0 = 160 kg·m.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: What does a tailwind do to landing distance?
questions.explain: A tailwind increases groundspeed at touchdown and lengthens the landing distance.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Flying above maximum take-off mass would…
options: Raise the stall speed, lengthen take-off and reduce climb
Have no effect if the runway is long
questions.explain: Excess mass degrades almost every aspect of performance and may exceed structural limits.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Applying carburettor heat with no ice present usually causes…
questions.explain: Warmer, less dense air richens the mixture and lowers power slightly. If ice is present, RPM may drop and then rise as it melts.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Why do piston aero engines have two magnetos?
options: For redundancy and more complete combustion
questions.explain: Each magneto fires its own set of plugs independently, so the engine keeps running if one fails.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: If the static source becomes blocked in flight, the altimeter will…
options: Freeze at the level where the blockage happened
questions.explain: With no change in static pressure, the altimeter freezes. The VSI shows zero and the ASI becomes inaccurate as altitude changes.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Why is the mixture leaned as you climb?
options: Because air density drops, so less fuel is needed for the correct ratio
questions.explain: Thinner air at altitude needs less fuel to keep the correct fuel-to-air ratio.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: In many light aircraft, which instruments are driven by the vacuum system?
questions.explain: The attitude and heading indicators are commonly vacuum-driven; the turn coordinator is often electric. Check your aircraft’s manual.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Why must the heading indicator be checked against the magnetic compass regularly?
options: It drifts over time because of gyroscopic precession
It only works on the ground
questions.explain: The heading indicator has no magnetic sensing and drifts, so realign it with the compass in steady flight.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: Which is a likely cause of high oil temperature in the climb?
options: Low airspeed and high power for a long time
questions.explain: High power with low cooling airflow raises temperatures. A lean mixture or low oil level can also cause it.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Using the 1 in 60 rule, if you are 1 NM off track after 60 NM, your track error is about…
questions.explain: The 1 in 60 rule: 1 NM off track in 60 NM is about 1° of error.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: What is magnetic variation?
options: The error caused by the aircraft’s own metal
The angle between true north and magnetic north
The difference between heading and track
A change in compass reading in turns
questions.explain: Variation is the angle between true and magnetic north, and it changes with location and time.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: True track is 090° and variation is 3° W. What is the magnetic track?
questions.explain: “Variation west, magnetic best”: add westerly variation, so 090 + 3 = 093°M.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: At a groundspeed of 120 kt, how long does it take to fly 30 NM?
questions.explain: 120 kt is 2 NM per minute, so 30 NM takes 15 minutes.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: How many metres are there in one nautical mile?
questions.explain: One nautical mile is 1,852 m, equal to one minute of latitude.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Compass deviation is caused by…
options: Magnetic fields in the aircraft itself
questions.explain: Deviation comes from the aircraft’s own metal and electrics, and is shown on the compass deviation card.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: The wind is blowing from your left across your track. To stay on track you should…
options: Head slightly left of track, into the wind
questions.explain: Turn the nose into the wind to offset drift. With wind from the left, head left of track.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: A VOR radial is…
options: A true bearing to the station
A magnetic bearing from the station
questions.explain: A radial is the magnetic bearing outbound from the VOR station.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: An aircraft is landing or on final approach. Which aircraft has right of way?
options: The aircraft landing or on final approach
questions.explain: Aircraft landing or in the final stages of an approach have right of way over other aircraft in flight or on the ground.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Two aeroplanes are approaching the same aerodrome to land. Which normally has right of way?
options: The lower one, as long as it doesn’t cut in front of one on final
questions.explain: The lower aircraft has right of way, but it must not use this to cut in front of another aircraft on final or overtake it.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Which transponder code indicates unlawful interference (a hijack)?
questions.explain: 7500 is unlawful interference, 7600 radio failure and 7700 emergency.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: In flight you see a steady green light from the tower aimed at you. What does it mean?
questions.explain: A steady green light to an aircraft in flight means cleared to land. Flashing green means return for landing.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: In flight you see a flashing red light from the tower. What does it mean?
questions.explain: Flashing red to an aircraft in flight means the aerodrome is unsafe, do not land.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: Who has final authority and responsibility for the operation and safety of the aircraft?
questions.explain: The pilot in command is directly responsible for, and has final authority over, the operation of the aircraft.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: What is a NOTAM?
options: A weather forecast for an aerodrome
A notice about a change to a facility, service, procedure or hazard
questions.explain: A NOTAM (Notice to Airmen/Air Missions) gives timely information on facilities, services, procedures or hazards that pilots need to know. Check them before every flight.

questions.subject: airlaw
questions.q: On the ground you see a steady red light from the tower. What should you do?
options: Taxi clear of the landing area
questions.explain: A steady red light to an aircraft on the ground means stop.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: How does alcohol affect a pilot’s tolerance of altitude?
options: It makes hypoxia more likely at lower altitudes
questions.explain: Alcohol reduces the body’s ability to use oxygen, so the effects of hypoxia appear at lower altitudes, and it impairs judgement on top.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: How long do your eyes take to adapt fully to darkness?
questions.explain: Full dark adaptation takes around 30 minutes, and a moment of bright white light can undo much of it.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What is empty-field myopia?
options: The eyes focusing at short range when there is nothing to focus on, such as a featureless sky
A blind spot caused by the windscreen pillar
questions.explain: With nothing to focus on, the eyes relax to a focus of a metre or two, so distant traffic is easily missed. Focus on a distant object from time to time while scanning.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Pressing on to your destination as the weather gets worse, because you’ve already come this far, is an example of…
questions.explain: Plan continuation bias makes us stick to the plan despite changing conditions. Decide your diversion and turn-back points before you go.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: What does the IMSAFE check cover?
options: Instruments, mixture, switches, altimeter, fuel, engine
Illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and eating or emotion
Inspection, maintenance, service, airworthiness, fuel, equipment
Ice, mist, snow, air, fog, electrical storms
questions.explain: IMSAFE is a personal fitness check before flying: illness, medication, stress, alcohol, fatigue and eating (or emotion).

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Why should you check before flying after taking an over-the-counter medicine?
options: Many cause drowsiness or other side effects that affect flying
They only matter for commercial pilots
questions.explain: Common medicines such as antihistamines can cause drowsiness or slowed reactions. Check with an aviation medical examiner if you’re unsure.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: Accelerating quickly on take-off in poor visibility, a pilot may feel the nose is pitching up when it isn’t. This is…
questions.explain: Linear acceleration feels like a nose-up pitch. A pilot who reacts by pushing forward can fly into the ground, so trust the instruments.

questions.subject: human
questions.q: In haze, how do objects such as other aircraft or the runway tend to appear?
options: Exactly as far as they are
questions.explain: Haze makes objects look further away than they really are, which can lead to a low approach.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What is the approximate dry adiabatic lapse rate?
questions.explain: Rising unsaturated air cools at about 3 °C per 1,000 ft (about 1 °C per 100 m).

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Which cloud type is associated with thunderstorms?
questions.explain: Cumulonimbus (CB) brings thunderstorms, with severe turbulence, icing, hail, lightning and wind shear. Keep well clear.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: What marks the mature stage of a thunderstorm?
options: Both updraughts and downdraughts, with precipitation reaching the ground
questions.explain: In the mature stage the storm has strong updraughts and downdraughts side by side and precipitation falls to the surface. It is the most dangerous stage.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: In a TAF, what does “TEMPO” mean?
options: Temporary changes, each lasting less than an hour and in total less than half the period
A forecast that has been amended
questions.explain: TEMPO groups describe temporary fluctuations: each lasts less than one hour and together they cover less than half the stated period.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: A METAR shows “24015G25KT”. What does this mean?
options: Wind from 240° at 15 kt, gusting 25 kt
questions.explain: The wind is from 240° (true, in a METAR) at 15 knots, with gusts to 25 knots.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: You fly from high pressure towards low pressure without resetting the altimeter. Where is the aircraft compared with what the altimeter shows?
options: It depends on the temperature only
questions.explain: “High to low, look out below”: the altimeter over-reads, so you are lower than it shows.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Moist, stable air is pushed up a slope. What kind of cloud forms?
questions.explain: Stable air forced to rise forms layered (stratiform) cloud, sometimes with drizzle. Unstable air builds cumuliform cloud.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: Airframe icing is most likely when flying…
options: In visible moisture at temperatures from about 0 °C to −15 °C
questions.explain: Structural icing needs visible moisture (cloud or rain) at or below freezing, and is most common from 0 °C down to about −15 °C.

questions.subject: met
questions.q: On a sunny day at the coast, which way does a sea breeze blow?
options: From the land out to sea
From the sea onto the land
questions.explain: The land heats faster than the sea in the day, so air rises over land and cooler sea air flows in. At night the land breeze reverses it.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “STANDBY” mean?
options: Wait and I will call you
questions.explain: Standby means wait and I will call you. It is not an approval or a clearance.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: How do you say an altitude of 2,500 ft on the radio?
questions.explain: ICAO phraseology says whole thousands and hundreds: “two thousand five hundred feet”. (US pilots also often hear “two thousand five hundred”.)

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which phrase asks the station to repeat its last message?
questions.explain: “Say again” asks for the message to be repeated. “Confirm” asks the other station to verify something.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Which call signals urgency, a serious situation that isn’t immediate grave danger?
questions.explain: PAN PAN is the urgency call, for example a sick passenger or a developing technical problem. MAYDAY is for grave and imminent danger.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: What does “NEGATIVE” mean?
options: No, or permission not granted, or that is not correct
questions.explain: “Negative” means no, permission not granted, or that is not correct.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: ATC asks you to “squawk ident”. What do you do?
options: Press the ident button on the transponder
questions.explain: Squawk ident means press the IDENT button, which highlights your return on the controller’s screen.

questions.subject: comms
questions.q: Your receiver has failed but you think the transmitter works. What should you do?
options: Transmit your intentions blind, prefixed “transmitting blind”
questions.explain: Make your calls as normal, prefixed “transmitting blind”, and squawk 7600, because ATC may still hear you.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: In straight, level, unaccelerated flight…
options: Lift equals weight and thrust equals drag
questions.explain: In steady level flight the forces are balanced: lift equals weight and thrust equals drag.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: How does induced drag change as airspeed decreases in level flight?
questions.explain: At low speed the wing needs a higher angle of attack, which creates more induced drag. Parasite drag does the opposite and grows with speed.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: If the aircraft is lighter, what happens to its stall speed?
questions.explain: Less weight needs less lift, so the wing reaches the critical angle of attack at a lower speed.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: The angle of attack is the angle between…
options: The wing chord line and the horizon
The wing chord line and the relative airflow
questions.explain: Angle of attack is measured between the chord line and the relative airflow, not the horizon.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Which two things are needed for a spin to develop?
options: High speed and a steep turn
A forward centre of gravity and low power
questions.explain: A spin needs the wing to be stalled and the aircraft yawing. Keeping the ball centred near the stall helps prevent one.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: If airspeed doubles at the same angle of attack, lift becomes about…
questions.explain: Lift is proportional to the square of the airspeed, so doubling speed gives about four times the lift.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: A heavier aircraft glides at its best glide speed. Compared with a lighter one, its glide…
options: Covers about the same distance, at a higher best glide speed
questions.explain: The best lift-to-drag ratio doesn’t depend on weight, so the glide angle and distance stay about the same; only the best glide speed is higher.

questions.subject: pof
questions.q: Parasite drag increases…
questions.explain: Parasite (form, skin friction and interference) drag grows with the square of airspeed.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: During a fuel check, how does water show up in the sample?
options: As a cloudy layer on top
As beads or a layer at the bottom
As a change of smell only
questions.explain: Water is heavier than fuel, so it sinks to the bottom of the sampler as beads or a clear layer. Keep sampling until it’s gone.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Before starting the engine you should…
options: Check the propeller area is clear and warn people nearby
questions.explain: Look all around, make sure the propeller area is clear and give a warning (such as “Clear prop!”) before starting.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: The engine fails after take-off or in flight. What is the first priority?
options: Fly the aircraft and set the best glide speed
questions.explain: Aviate, navigate, communicate: keep control and set best glide speed first, then choose a field and work through the checks.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Why fly an inspection run before a precautionary landing?
options: To check the landing surface, obstacles and approach
To warn people on the ground
Because it is always required by ATC
questions.explain: Flying over the chosen area lets you check the surface, slope, obstacles and approach path before committing to land.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: What makes an approach “stabilised”?
options: Any approach that ends on the runway
On the correct path, at the right speed and configuration, with steady power, by a set point
questions.explain: A stabilised approach is on path, on speed, in the landing configuration with stable power by a set point. If it isn’t, go around.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Why check that the fuel caps are secure before flight?
options: A loose cap can let fuel siphon out in flight
questions.explain: Low pressure over the wing can siphon fuel through an unsecured cap, and you may lose a lot of fuel quickly.

questions.subject: ops
questions.q: Which runway condition makes aquaplaning (hydroplaning) most likely?
questions.explain: Standing water lets tyres ride on a film of water, so braking and steering become poor.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How does a higher aircraft mass affect take-off distance?
questions.explain: A heavier aircraft accelerates more slowly and needs a higher lift-off speed, so it needs more runway.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: What does an upslope runway do to take-off distance?
questions.explain: Taking off uphill slows the acceleration, so take-off distance increases.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: The wind is 20 kt at 60° to the runway. What is the approximate crosswind component?
questions.explain: Crosswind = wind speed × sin(angle). sin 60° ≈ 0.87, so about 17 kt.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: An aircraft burns 30 litres an hour. How much fuel does a 1 hour 20 minute flight use, before reserves?
questions.explain: 1 h 20 min is 1⅓ hours, and 30 × 1⅓ = 40 litres. Then add your required reserves and contingency.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: At a high density altitude, what happens to engine power and propeller efficiency?
questions.explain: Thinner air means a normally aspirated engine makes less power and the propeller bites less air, so performance drops.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Compared with an aft centre of gravity, a forward centre of gravity gives…
options: Lower stall speed and lighter controls
Higher stall speed, more stability and heavier elevator
questions.explain: With a forward CG the tail must push down harder, which raises the stall speed slightly, adds stability and makes the elevator heavier.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: How does wet grass affect landing distance?
options: It lengthens it, because braking is poorer
questions.explain: Wet grass gives much less braking friction, so the landing roll is longer. Use the POH factors for surface and condition.

questions.subject: perf
questions.q: Why add safety factors to figures from the performance charts?
options: The charts assume a new aircraft flown by an expert in ideal conditions
Safety factors are only for jets
questions.explain: Chart figures come from test flying in ideal conditions. Real aircraft, pilots and surfaces do worse, so factors give a margin.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: In flight the ammeter shows a discharge. What does this suggest?
options: The alternator isn’t charging and the battery is supplying the load
questions.explain: A discharge usually means the alternator has stopped charging. Reduce the electrical load and follow the checklist: the battery won’t last long.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: The pitot tube and its drain hole become blocked and you climb. What does the airspeed indicator do?
options: Reads higher, acting like an altimeter
questions.explain: With the pitot pressure trapped, falling static pressure in the climb makes the ASI over-read, like an altimeter.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What does moving the mixture to idle cut-off do?
options: Stops fuel flow to stop the engine
questions.explain: Idle cut-off stops fuel reaching the engine. It is the normal way to shut down a piston engine.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What is detonation?
options: Explosive, uncontrolled combustion of the fuel-air mixture
questions.explain: Detonation is explosive combustion in the cylinder, made more likely by high temperatures, an over-lean mixture or the wrong fuel. It can damage the engine quickly.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: What colour is AVGAS 100LL?
questions.explain: 100LL is dyed blue. Checking the colour helps catch the wrong fuel.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: In a turn the slip ball sits out to the right. What should you do?
questions.explain: “Step on the ball”: apply rudder on the side the ball has moved to, here right rudder, to centre it.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: With QNH set on the altimeter, what does it show?
questions.explain: QNH gives altitude above mean sea level. QFE gives height above the aerodrome; 1013 hPa gives pressure altitude.

questions.subject: agk
questions.q: In the northern hemisphere, accelerating on an east or west heading, the magnetic compass shows…
questions.explain: Acceleration error: accelerate, the compass shows a turn north; decelerate, it shows a turn south (ANDS), in the northern hemisphere.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: How many nautical miles are in one degree of latitude?
questions.explain: One degree of latitude is 60 NM, and one minute of latitude is 1 NM.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: At 90 kt groundspeed, how long does 45 NM take?
questions.explain: 90 kt is 1.5 NM a minute, so 45 NM takes 30 minutes.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: True heading is 270° and variation is 5° E. What is the magnetic heading?
questions.explain: “Variation east, magnetic least”: subtract easterly variation, so 270 − 5 = 265°.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Isogonals are lines joining places of equal…
questions.explain: Isogonals join points of equal magnetic variation. The agonic line joins points of zero variation.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: On a 1:500,000 chart, what does 1 cm represent?

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: You become unsure of your position. What should you do first?
options: Keep flying the aircraft on a sensible heading, check fuel and time, and ask for help if needed
Turn back immediately whatever the fuel state
Switch off the radio to concentrate
questions.explain: Stay calm and fly the aircraft, note the time and fuel, use your planned heading and checkpoints to work out where you are, and ask ATC for help early.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: You set off at 10:00 to fly 40 NM at a groundspeed of 120 kt. What is your ETA?
questions.explain: 120 kt is 2 NM a minute, so 40 NM takes 20 minutes: ETA 10:20.

questions.subject: nav
questions.q: Flight levels are based on which altimeter setting?
questions.explain: Flight levels use the standard pressure setting so all aircraft at the level share the same reference.
